beats.intro: Chapter five. [[sub]]We rarely see a whole population. Sampling and estimation tell us how far we can trust what a sample says.
beats.sampling: [[a]]A population is everything we want to know about. A sample is the part we actually observe. [[pop]]Here is a population of one hundred values, with a true mean we call mu. [[s1]]Draw a random sample, and its mean estimates mu. [[s2]]Draw another, and we get a different answer. [[s3]]And another. [[dist]]Sample means vary from sample to sample, and that variation has a distribution of its own: the sampling distribution.
beats.clt: [[a]]The central limit theorem says that for large samples, the sample mean is approximately normal, whatever the shape of the population. It centers on the population mean, with a standard deviation of sigma over the square root of n. [[pop]]Here the population has a standard deviation of ten. [[n4]]With four observations, the standard error is five. [[n25]]With twenty-five, two. [[n100]]With one hundred, just one. [[note]]Bigger samples give tighter estimates, but slowly: to halve the error, we need four times the data.
beats.se: [[a]]In practice we do not know sigma, so we use the sample standard deviation, s. The standard error of the sample mean is s divided by the square root of n. [[ex]]With s equal to twelve and thirty-six observations, that is twelve over six: two. [[ci]]A confidence interval is the estimate, plus or minus a reliability factor, times the standard error. [[z]]For ninety-five percent confidence, the factor is one point nine six. With a sample mean of eight percent, the interval is eight plus or minus three point nine two: from four point oh eight to eleven point nine two.
beats.q1: Quick check. Find the standard error.
beats.ci: [[a]]What does ninety-five percent confidence really mean? [[draw]]Imagine drawing twenty different samples from the same population, each with its own interval. [[hit]]Nineteen of the twenty intervals capture the true mean. [[miss]]One misses. [[rule]]In the long run, ninety-five percent of such intervals contain the true mean. A given interval either does or does not, but the procedure is right ninety-five percent of the time. With a small sample and unknown variance, we use a t factor instead of one point nine six.
beats.samplesize: [[a]]How big should a sample be? The margin of error is the reliability factor times s over the square root of n. [[solve]]Solve for n: n equals the factor times s, over the margin, squared. [[ex]]For ninety-five percent confidence, s of twelve, and a margin of two: one point nine six times twelve over two, squared, is about one hundred thirty-eight point three. [[up]]We always round up: one hundred thirty-nine observations. [[note]]Halving the margin needs four times the sample.
beats.q2: Quick check. Find the sample size.
beats.biases: [[a]]Even a perfect formula cannot fix a bad sample. Four biases to watch. [[ds]]Data snooping: testing many ideas on the same data until one looks good. [[ss]]Sample selection bias: the sample leaves out part of the population, as when funds that closed are missing. That is survivorship bias. [[la]]Look-ahead bias: using information that was not available on the date of the decision. [[tp]]Time-period bias: the sample period is too short, or too unusual, to represent the long run.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Sample means vary, and their distribution is the sampling distribution. [[w2]]By the central limit theorem, it is approximately normal with a standard error of s over root n. [[w3]]A confidence interval is the estimate plus or minus a reliability factor times the standard error. [[w4]]Watch for data snooping, selection, look-ahead and time-period biases. [[end]]Now try the chapter practice.
beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of chapter five.
